storm.summary_layperson: No storms anywhere nearby tonight — clear skies and a light southwest breeze, so there's nothing for the Sound to protect the cove from.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Sound water (60°F) is already only 4°F cooler than the air at 4 PM — below the ~5°F needed for a protective marine layer — and the air drops to the water's temperature by about 7 PM, so there's no buffer this evening (and nothing on radar that needs one).
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: quiet. KOKX radar shows no echoes anywhere in range, the atmosphere has zero instability (CAPE 0 J/kg), and wind shear is a modest 16 kt from the west. High pressure (about 1020 hPa) covers the area with a steady light southwest flow from New York Harbor to Block Island. The NWS forecast calls for mostly clear skies tonight with a low around 53°F.

The one active NWS product is not about storms. A Special Weather Statement covers an elevated fire-spread risk across southern Connecticut on Friday late morning and afternoon, when gusty northwest winds of 20–30 mph combine with dry fuels and relative humidity near 40%. Nothing in it applies to this evening, but take care with any outdoor burning or grills tomorrow.

Local effect — none in play. On summer afternoons the cool Sound sets up a stable marine layer that often weakens storms as they cross the water. That needs the air to be at least ~5°F warmer than the water. Today the Sound is 60°F and the cove air is about 64°F, a gap of only 4°F at 4 PM. The Sound holds its temperature while the air cools after the 5:53 PM sunset, so the gap keeps closing: about 3°F by 5 PM, and by about 7 PM the air is as cool as the water or cooler. There is no protective layer this evening, but with no storms around it doesn't matter.

Cove vs. surrounding areas: same as everyone else — dry and calm. No meaningful difference between the waterfront and inland towns tonight.

What would change the call: very little. Nothing convective is expected. The next weather feature is a wind shift to the west and northwest on Friday, which brings drier, gusty air rather than storms.

wind.regime_label: Light southwest gradient wind — no sea breeze
wind.tactics_blurb: Light, steady SSW–SW breeze that dips to about 4 kt around sunset, then fills back to 6–7 kt after dark. Southwesterly winds spread evenly across the cove, so stay in the middle, sail for pressure over angle in the 6 PM lull, and lean right later as it veers toward SW around 10 PM.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
What kind of day: a light gradient wind, with no sea breeze in play. Every station from Westchester to Block Island, Boston and Providence shows the same southwest flow, so this is the large-scale (gradient) wind, not a local thermal. A sea breeze needs the land to be at least ~5°F warmer than the water. Today the gap between the air and the Sound is only 4.3°F (air 64°F, water 60°F), and the late-October sun is too weak to drive one. Well-sited anemometers around the region average 8.5 kt right now, and RYC reads 8.6 kt (10-min average) from the SSW with gusts to 12.

Through the evening: it softens, but gradient wind doesn't switch off at sunset the way a sea breeze does. The model (HRRR) has the breeze easing to about 6 kt by 5 PM and bottoming out near 4 kt around 6 PM, just after the 5:53 PM sunset, as the air near the ground settles. It then fills back to 6–7 kt from the SSW between 7 and 10 PM, in line with the NWS overnight call of southwest around 8 mph. After dark the air drops below the 60°F water temperature, so the air over the Sound stays mixed and the breeze on the water should hold up better than the inland stations suggest.

Where the pressure is: SSW–SW comes straight in from the Sound with only a little channeling along the west shore, so pressure is fairly even across the cove. If anything it is slightly stronger toward the mouth and the east (Tod's Point) side, which has less shelter. In this light air, finding pressure matters more than playing small direction changes.

Shift character: mostly steady, with normal light-air puffs and lulls. Two things to watch: a brief swing toward SW (about 229°) around the 6 PM lull, and a slow, lasting veer from SSW back toward SW by about 10 PM. Once that late veer starts, the right side pays. Direction across the region is consistent (79% agreement), so big unexplained shifts are unlikely.

What the fleet will feel: heavier boats will struggle in the 6 PM lull at around 4 kt, but 6–7 kt after 7 PM is enough for light-air racing. Expect most gusts in the 8–9 kt range. Tomorrow's west-to-northwest shift arrives well after this window.
